findings.title: Beyond weaponized interdependence: the corporate chokehold in frontier semiconductor governance
findings.abstract_or_evidence: Peer-reviewed theory-testing process-tracing study of the ASML–TSMC frontier semiconductor production system. The author analyses corporate and government documentation to distinguish state control of access (export licensing and restrictions) from firm control of lithography servicing, qualification and advanced-packaging production schedules. The author reports a 204-document purposively selected corpus and an infrastructural-embedment, authority-relocation, temporal-lock-in framework. Publication title, author, DOI and 20 August 2026 online date checked on the original Taylor & Francis page.
principal_findings: Dutch ASML controls an essential leading-edge EUV lithography equipment-and-servicing gate; Taiwan-based TSMC controls frontier design qualification, advanced packaging and capacity allocation, creating an interdependent production bottleneck.

Export controls and onshoring can alter who may access frontier semiconductors without automatically transferring operational authority from specialized vendors; these are case-based mechanism findings, not a quantitative causal effect estimate.
findings.eu_economic_security_relevance: The study directly investigates economic-security exposure tied to ASML, a Netherlands-based strategic technology supplier, including Dutch export licensing, transatlantic coordination, and the limits of industrial policy to secure frontier semiconductor production.
evidence_quotes: Why can states restrict adversaries’ access to frontier semiconductors yet not
ASML, a Dutch company, controls the lithography tools and service regime

findings.title: Friend or Foe? Analysing Neutral States' Exports to the Russian Federation Using Synthetic Difference-In-Differences
findings.abstract_or_evidence: Original empirical journal article, first online 24 June 2026. Uses UN Comtrade and 13 synthetic difference-in-differences panel models to assess 2018–2024 monthly exports to Russia from nine non-sanctioning or comparatively neutral countries, comparing product groups targeted by European sanctions with other traded goods. The publisher explicitly identifies only Kazakhstan and Türkiye as statistically significant in the reported changes.
principal_findings: The reported value of sanctioned commodity exports to Russia increased in nine relevant model instances; significant modeled changes occurred in Kazakhstan and Türkiye, not uniformly across all examined partners.
The observed redirection is consistent with sanctions-circumvention risk for European restrictions, but aggregate trade patterns alone do not establish illicit intent of individual firms.
findings.eu_economic_security_relevance: Direct test of whether flows through third countries can undermine EU export restrictions imposed against Russia. It supplies original cross-border trade evidence useful for European sanctions enforcement and anti-circumvention design.
evidence_quotes: The research is based on 13 synthetic difference-in-difference panel data models
The results highlight an increase in the value of sanctioned commodities

findings.title: Regulating Source Code in Trade Agreements: Between Protection and Disclosure
findings.abstract_or_evidence: Cambridge original research article first published online 28 September 2026. Legal and comparative examination of digital-trade source-code non-disclosure rules, including evidence and coding of provisions across 39 free-trade and digital economic agreements. Discusses interaction of EU bilateral digital-trade texts and EU AI Act disclosure, audit and market-surveillance powers. The claim is institutional/legal analysis, not an empirical estimate of economic losses.
principal_findings: Source-code non-disclosure clauses provide ex-ante protections beyond traditional intellectual property law and can constrain the space in which regulators obtain code or algorithm access.

The shape of exceptions and carve-outs is particularly consequential for reconciling technology-transfer protection with legitimate regulatory transparency and AI oversight, including EU agreements and EU AI Act obligations.
findings.eu_economic_security_relevance: Examines forced technology-transfer prevention, algorithmic dependence and the policy autonomy of European digital regulators. The original study explicitly discusses EU–Korea and EU–Singapore digital-trade agreements and potential tension with the EU AI Act.

findings.title: Strengthening the EU’s Medical Supply Chains
findings.abstract_or_evidence: OECD Health Policy Studies, 277 pages, with subtitle International Co-operation and New Technologies for Better Emergency Preparedness, official publication date 22 September 2026. Maps EU supply chains for injectable corticosteroids, influenza vaccines and RT-PCR diagnostic tests and investigates dependence on suppliers, manufacturing concentration and evidence gaps. Tests the policy feasibility of international co-operation instruments and traceability/demand-monitoring technology.
principal_findings: OECD reports 84 sellers of injectable corticosteroids in the EU but commonly one or two main suppliers per national molecule market, and five major seasonal-influenza-vaccine manufacturers; these market counts do not directly measure upstream supply volumes.

In its EU steroid case, 20 API certified supplying firms were identified: six located in the EU, nine in China, two in India, two in the United States and one in Malaysia; country volume contributions were not established.
The study favours selective cooperation, diversified procurement and improved visibility rather than unsupported blanket reshoring, while cautioning that survey response rates were low.
findings.eu_economic_security_relevance: A direct, empirically supported study of EU dependence on foreign medical inputs and supplier concentration, with policy assessments of European strategic stockpiling, international procurement, trade facilitation and crisis resilience.
evidence_quotes: It supports ongoing European initiatives on medical supply chains and preparedness
including measures to expand manufacturing capacity and diversify supply, promote regulatory alignment

findings.title: The EU automotive industry at a crossroads
findings.abstract_or_evidence: Joint OECD–European Commission 33-page institutional policy-research paper, subtitle The implications of structural transformation for employment and skills, officially dated 30 September 2026. Analyses EU automotive supply chains, 2008–2025 employment and skills transitions under electrification, China competition and digital technology dependency. It reports intermediate-input sourcing from within the EU rising from 18% to 25% over 1995–2025.
principal_findings: EU automotive production and supplier employment declined after 2019 despite roughly stable sector-wide employment 2008–2025, with a shift towards central/eastern European activities.
Intra-EU sourcing of intermediate inputs rose from 18% in 1995 to 25% in 2025 while dependence on China increased for batteries and advanced electronics.

The paper reports substantial skills-transition risks among automotive manufacturing workers; the skills analysis is relevant to resilience but should not substitute for economic-security supply evidence.
findings.eu_economic_security_relevance: The paper provides EU-specific evidence on industrial capability, battery and advanced electronics dependencies on China, and the resilience of European automotive manufacturing supply chains under global technological rivalry.
evidence_quotes: The European Union’s automotive sector employs more than 6 million workers
alongside growing dependencies on China for batteries and advanced electronics

findings.title: Enhancing Resilience Through Traceability
findings.abstract_or_evidence: Official OECD report, 132 pages, subtitle Insights from Lithium and Nickel Supply Chains in Latin America and Southeast Asia, published 9 September 2026. OECD–IEA industry survey of 90 companies plus interviews and site visits on Chilean/Argentine lithium and Indonesian/Philippine nickel supply systems. Assesses mineral chain-of-custody tools, ownership opacity and traceability costs with recommendations explicitly connected to EU Critical Raw Materials Act requirements and the EU Battery Regulation.
principal_findings: The industry survey indicates fragmented traceability: participating companies face interoperability, cost, confidentiality and ultimate ownership problems that hinder supply-chain risk monitoring.

Dependence on China-linked processing remains important for Latin American lithium. End-to-end material tracking is not always practical; the report proposes targeted risk-sensitive mapping, supplier verification and interoperable data for sensitive downstream uses.

The OECD report discusses European Critical Raw Materials Act requirements and links data mapping to EU sourcing and regulatory resilience; it does not claim to quantify the EU share of each studied mineral stream.
findings.eu_economic_security_relevance: Substantive supply-risk and mineral-security research relevant to the EU Critical Raw Materials Act and EU battery supply-chain rules. The OECD study itself discusses EU supply-chain risk assessments and policy tools for securing raw-material inputs, even though its case studies are in Latin America and Southeast Asia.
